messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

When Roberto first spoke about the violence in his marriage, he did so in a flat, almost puzzled way, as if he were describing something that had happened to another man. He is a 72-year-old Southeast Asian American who has spent the last several years working as a nanny for a family with two young children, and he still seemed embarrassed by how frightened he had been inside his own home. The worst incident had happened at night. His wife had cornered him in a dark hallway after an argument, and when he tried to step past her she struck him and forced him down, leaving him pinned and twisted in a way he can still feel in his body. What remains most vivid is not a sequence he can calmly tell from beginning to end, but the terror of being trapped in the dark with sudden movement coming toward him. Even now, when he tries to recall it, he says the fear arrives at full strength, and his shoulders pull in and his torso stiffens as though he is back in that position on the floor. At times the scene feels strangely unreal to him, as if it belongs to someone else and not to the older man sitting in the office trying to explain it.

In the months after that assault, Roberto began to organize his life around not setting off those memories. Because remembering brought back the same terror and the same bodily sense of being pinned, he stopped allowing himself to feel angry at all; anger seemed too close to the argument that had preceded the assault, too likely to pull him back into it. He also became careful about avoiding reminders, especially darkness, and more generally started steering away from anything that might feel stressful. He described this not as cowardice but as common sense: if stress, conflict, or certain situations could make the memory come alive in his body, then it felt safer to stay quiet, keep the peace, and not go near anything that might stir it up.

Those memories also left him living as though danger were still close by. The moment the event comes to mind, his body braces, and outside those moments he has been unable to fully relax even when he knows he is safe. At the house where he works, this has become painfully obvious. If one of the children runs past him unexpectedly or darts into his side vision, he reacts with a sharp jolt, sometimes stepping back or throwing up an arm before he can stop himself. Sudden movement nearby feels to him like threat before his mind has time to catch up. He is easily startled by small noises and quick gestures, and because his body remains so tense, ordinary days never quite feel ordinary.

That constant sense of danger has, in turn, narrowed his life further. Since he feels jumpy and unable to settle, Roberto tries to manage himself by avoiding circumstances that might leave him exposed or overwhelmed. He keeps lights on in rooms even during the day if they seem dim, hesitates to take the children into darker play areas, and avoids outings that seem unpredictable or noisy. He has become intensely cautious about stress of any kind; even minor disagreements with the parents he works for are swallowed immediately. He is especially determined never to show anger. In his mind, if he lets himself feel it, his body will surge into the same state of alarm and he will lose the little control he has.

Yet these strategies have not quieted the past. The more Roberto pushes anger down and arranges his days to avoid reminders and stress, the more strange and intrusive the memory has become. Because he does not speak about what happened and cuts himself off whenever irritation or resentment arises, the experience remains unprocessed, returning in abrupt fragments rather than as something finished. He notices this most in the evenings, when he has spent the whole day carefully composed: a flash of the hallway comes back with a force that feels borrowed and alien, and his body folds inward before he has even fully pictured why. Avoiding darkness helps him for a moment, but it also keeps darkness charged; suppressing anger spares him the feeling in the short term, but the memory returns untouched, still carrying terror.

Lately the cycle has tightened enough that he could no longer dismiss it as simply aging or nerves. After one of the children rushed up behind him in a dim hallway and he flinched so violently that the child began to cry, Roberto went home shaken and ashamed. He realized how much of each day was spent bracing, scanning, and trying not to feel. He has come for help because he is afraid that if this continues he will withdraw from work and from the small, careful life he has built. What he hopes for, quietly, is to be able to stand in a dark room, feel a stir of anger or stress, and still know that he is here now and no longer there.
